index.title: MapleSteps: free guide for newcomers to Canada
index.desc: Free, plain-language guide for newcomers and immigrants to Canada: first steps, housing, jobs, health care, banking and taxes.
index.h1: Your first months in Canada, one step at a time
index.lead: Plain-language guides for newcomers and immigrants. Free, independent, and linked to official sources.
index.guides_lead: Start with the checklist, then read what you need now.
numbers: Police, fire or ambulance. Free from any phone.
Food, housing, settlement and other local services.
Talk to a nurse in most provinces. Not for emergencies.
index.free_h: Free settlement help is near you
index.free_p: Government-funded organizations across Canada help newcomers find housing, jobs, language classes and schools. Many have staff who speak your language, and most services are free for permanent residents and refugees.

first-steps.card: A checklist for your first weeks, in the right order.
first-steps.title: First steps in Canada: newcomer checklist
first-steps.desc: A step-by-step checklist for your first weeks in Canada: SIN, health card, bank account, phone, settlement services, school, benefits and taxes.
first-steps.lead: Tick off each step as you go. Most can be done in your first two weeks, and settlement workers can help with any of them for free.
checklist: Store your passport, Confirmation of Permanent Residence or permit, and landing papers somewhere safe. Keep copies and photos.
Apply for your Social Insurance Number (SIN)
You need a SIN to work and to get government benefits. Apply online or at a Service Canada office. It is free.
Apply for your provincial health card
Apply as soon as you arrive. Some provinces have a waiting period, so buy private insurance to cover it.
Bring your passport and immigration document. Ask about newcomer accounts with no monthly fee.
Compare prepaid and monthly plans. A local number helps with job applications and appointments.
They help with housing, jobs, forms and language classes, usually for free.
Public school is free. Contact your local school board with your children's documents.
Newcomers can apply to the Canada Revenue Agency for payments like the Canada child benefit and the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (formerly the GST/HST credit).
Each province has its own rules for exchanging a foreign licence. Some countries' licences can be exchanged directly.
Eligible newcomers can take free English or French classes. Ask your settlement agency.

sections.h: Before you start: what to carry
sections.p: Most first-week appointments ask for the same few documents. Keep them together in one folder and bring the whole folder each time.
items: Your passport and your Confirmation of Permanent Residence, work permit or study permit
Your permanent resident card once it arrives by mail (it can take several weeks)
Proof of your Canadian address, such as a lease or a letter from the person you stay with
Birth and marriage certificates, translated into English or French if needed
School records and vaccination records for your children

sections.p: Your Social Insurance Number is a nine-digit number used for work, taxes and benefits. Applying is free, online or at a Service Canada office. Give it to your employer, your bank and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Do not give it to a landlord or a store, and never share it by text or email with someone who contacted you first.

sections.h: Settlement services are free. Use them
sections.p: Government-funded settlement agencies exist in almost every city. Staff can help you fill in forms, find housing, prepare for job interviews, enrol in language classes and register your children for school. Many speak Arabic, Chinese, Hindi, Persian and other languages. Services funded by the federal government are free for permanent residents and resettled refugees, and some provinces fund services for temporary residents too.

sections.h: Benefits you may be able to get
items: Canada child benefit: a monthly, tax-free payment for families with children under 18
Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (formerly the GST/HST credit): a payment every three months for people with low or modest income
Provincial benefits that come automatically with the federal ones in many provinces
In your first year, you apply with special CRA forms for newcomers. After that, filing your tax return every year keeps the payments coming

sections.p: You file your first Canadian tax return in the spring after you arrive, usually by April 30. You report your world income only from the day you became a resident. Even with little or no income, filing matters: it is how the CRA calculates your benefits and how you start building room for savings plans. Free tax clinics can file a simple return for you.

items: Keep a folder with copies of every form you send and every letter you get.
Government agencies never ask for payment by gift card, crypto or wire transfer.
When you move, update your address with IRCC, your bank and the CRA.
Your first months are busy. It is fine to do these steps one at a time.
How long does it take to get a SIN? If you apply in person with the right documents, you usually get your number the same day. Online applications can take longer.
Can I do these steps before I have a permanent address? Yes for most of them. Use the address where you are staying and update it when you move.
Do I need to speak English or French to get help? No. Settlement agencies often have staff who speak your language or can find an interpreter.
Which step matters most in week one? Your SIN and your health card application, because other steps (work, benefits and coverage) depend on them.

housing.card: Where to look, what landlords ask for, and how to avoid scams.
housing.title: Renting a home in Canada: guide for newcomers
housing.desc: How newcomers can find a place to rent in Canada, what landlords ask for, tenant rights and how to avoid rental scams.
housing.lead: Most newcomers start by renting. Prices, deposits and tenant rules depend on your city and province, so plan early, compare options and ask for help.

sections.p: Many newcomers book a furnished room, a short-term rental or a stay with family for the first few weeks. It gives you time to learn the neighbourhoods, open a bank account and see apartments in person before you sign a one-year lease.

items: Online rental listings and local community groups
Your settlement agency, which may know newcomer-friendly landlords
Property management companies, which often rent many units in the same building
Rooms in shared homes, which cost much less in expensive cities like Toronto and Vancouver
Signs in the windows of buildings in the neighbourhood you want
A rental application with your income or job offer
References from past landlords or employers, including from your home country
A credit check. With no Canadian credit yet, offer bank statements, a job letter or a guarantor as proof you can pay
A deposit. What a landlord can legally ask for depends on your province

sections.h: Deposits: the rules are different in each province
sections.p: Check your province before you pay anything. A few examples: in Ontario, a landlord can ask for a deposit of last month's rent but not a damage deposit. In British Columbia, a security deposit can be at most half of one month's rent. In Quebec, a landlord can ask for the first month's rent but no other deposit. If a landlord asks for more than the law allows, you can contact your province's tenant office.

items: Ask whether heat, hydro (electricity), water and internet are included
Tenant insurance is cheap and many leases require it. It protects your belongings and covers you if you cause damage
Some buildings charge extra for parking, storage or laundry
Winter heating bills can be high in older houses if heat is not included
Ask for a written lease and read it before you sign. In Ontario, most landlords must use the province's standard lease form
Each province has its own tenant rules and an office that settles disputes
A landlord cannot refuse you because of your race, religion, country of origin or family status, including having children
Keep a receipt for every payment and take dated photos of the unit when you move in
Never send money before you see the place and meet the landlord
Be careful when the rent is much lower than similar homes nearby
Don't share your passport or SIN until you have signed a lease. A landlord does not need your SIN
Pay in a way that leaves a record, never by gift card or crypto
Can I rent without a job in Canada? Yes. Many newcomers do. Show savings, a job offer or a guarantor, and some landlords accept a few months of rent paid in advance where the law allows it.
How long is a typical lease? Usually one year. After that, it often continues month to month on the same terms.
Can my landlord raise the rent at any time? No. Rules on how often and how much rent can go up are set by each province, and notice must be given in writing.
What if my landlord won't fix something? Ask in writing first and keep a copy. If nothing happens, contact your province's tenant office or a settlement worker.

work.card: Job search, Canadian-style résumés and licensed professions.
work.title: Finding work in Canada: guide for newcomers
work.desc: How newcomers can find a job in Canada: official job boards, Canadian-style résumés, licensed professions and your rights at work.
work.lead: A first Canadian job often comes through people you meet. Combine official job boards, free employment programs and every connection you have, and start licensing early if your profession is regulated.

items: Job Bank, the Government of Canada's free job board
Free employment programs at settlement agencies, including mentoring, job fairs and résumé reviews
Networking: tell friends, neighbours, faith groups and community groups what work you want
Professional associations in your field, many with newcomer memberships
Volunteering, which builds Canadian experience and references
Keep it to one or two pages, starting with your most recent job
Leave out your photo, age, marital status and religion
Show results with numbers where you can
Use the keywords from the job posting, because many employers scan résumés with software
Write a short cover letter for each job

sections.p: Canadian interviews often ask you to describe a time you solved a problem, worked in a team or handled a conflict. Prepare a few short stories that show the situation, what you did and the result. Arrive a few minutes early, research the employer, and send a short thank-you email afterward. Settlement agencies offer free mock interviews.

items: Doctors, nurses, engineers, teachers, accountants and many trades need a licence from a provincial regulator
Start the licensing process early, even before you arrive
You may need your education assessed and to pass exams or supervised practice
Bridging programs at colleges and settlement agencies help you return to your field faster
While you work toward your licence, look for related jobs in your field

sections.p: Your employer deducts income tax, Canada Pension Plan (or Quebec Pension Plan) contributions and Employment Insurance premiums from every pay cheque. Your take-home pay is usually much lower than your salary, so check the real number before you accept an offer. Our free pay calculator shows it for your province.

items: Each province sets its own minimum wage, overtime and vacation rules
You should get a pay stub that shows your hours and deductions
You can refuse work that is unsafe
An employer cannot make you pay to get a job or keep your passport
If you are injured at work, report it right away. Workplace insurance may cover your lost pay and treatment
Do I need Canadian experience to get hired? Many employers prefer it, but it is not a legal requirement. Volunteering, short contracts and bridging programs help you get it quickly.

Should I take a job outside my field at first? Many newcomers do while they network and finish licensing. Try to keep one foot in your field through courses, volunteering or a professional association.
Is an educational credential assessment the same as a licence? No. An assessment says how your degree compares to a Canadian one. Only the regulator in your province can license you.
What if I'm not paid for my work? Contact your province's employment standards office. You can make a complaint even if you no longer work there.

health.card: Get your health card, find a doctor and know what is covered.
health.title: Health care in Canada: guide for newcomers
health.desc: How health care works for newcomers to Canada: provincial health cards, waiting periods, what is covered and how to find a doctor.
health.lead: Each province and territory runs its own public health insurance plan. Apply for your card as soon as you arrive, plan for any waiting period, and learn where to go for different kinds of care.

items: Apply to your province or territory's health plan right after you arrive
Ontario has no waiting period for most newcomers. Several other provinces make you wait up to three months
Buy private insurance to cover any waiting period, ideally before you land
Resettled refugees and refugee claimants may get temporary coverage from the federal government
Carry your card to every appointment and renew it before it expires
Medically necessary doctor visits and hospital care
Usually not covered for most adults: dental care, glasses, physiotherapy and many prescriptions
Employer benefit plans often cover these extras
Some provinces have programs for children, seniors and low-income families
Family doctor or nurse practitioner: for regular check-ups and ongoing care. Register on your province's waiting list as soon as you have your card
Walk-in clinics: for non-urgent problems while you wait for a family doctor
Pharmacists: in many provinces, they can now prescribe for minor problems like urinary tract infections or pink eye
811: in most provinces, call to speak with a nurse day or night
911 or the emergency room: only for emergencies such as chest pain, trouble breathing or serious injury

sections.p: The Canadian Dental Care Plan helps residents with no dental insurance and a family income under a set limit. To qualify, you must have filed a tax return in Canada, which is one more reason to file every year. For prescriptions, some provinces have drug plans for low-income residents, and Quebec requires everyone to have drug insurance, either through work or the public plan.

items: Moving to a new country is stressful. Asking for help is normal
Call or text 988 at any time if you are thinking about suicide
Settlement agencies can connect you with counsellors who speak your language
Many employers offer a free, confidential assistance program for you and your family
Is health care free in Canada? Doctor and hospital care is paid by your provincial plan once you are covered. You will pay for most dental, vision and prescription costs unless you have insurance.
Can I see a doctor before my health card arrives? Yes, but you may have to pay. Keep your receipts, because private insurance may pay you back.
Can I use my health card in another province? For short trips, doctor and hospital care is usually covered. If you move, you must apply in your new province.
Do I need to bring my vaccination records? Yes. Schools ask for children's records, and they help your new doctor.

money.card: Banking, building credit, taxes and benefits.
money.title: Banking, credit and taxes for newcomers to Canada
money.desc: A newcomer's guide to banking in Canada, building a credit history, filing taxes, getting benefits and avoiding scams.
money.lead: A few early steps make life much easier: a bank account, a credit history, filing your taxes every year and knowing how to spot scams.

items: Most banks offer newcomer accounts with no monthly fee in the first year
You have the right to open a personal account with valid ID, even without a job or money to deposit
A chequing account is for daily spending; a savings account is for saving
Compare monthly fees and transaction limits before you choose, and check what happens when the newcomer offer ends
Eligible deposits at member institutions are protected up to $100,000 per category by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation
Your credit history starts at zero in Canada
A secured or newcomer credit card is an easy way to start
Pay the full balance on time every month, and use only a small part of your limit
Check your credit report for free with Equifax and TransUnion
Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA): earnings and withdrawals are tax-free. You get room starting in the year you become a resident, if you are 18 or older
Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP): contributions lower your taxes. Your room is based on income you earned in Canada, so it usually starts in your second year
First Home Savings Account (FHSA): for first-time home buyers who want to save for a down payment
Ask your bank for the official rules before you open one, and avoid going over your limit
File a tax return every year, even with no income, to keep getting benefits
The deadline for most people is April 30. Self-employed people have until June 15 to file but must still pay by April 30
In Quebec, you also file a provincial return with Revenu Québec
In your first year, you can apply for benefits before you file
Free tax clinics can file a simple return for you
Set up direct deposit with the CRA so payments arrive faster
The CRA never asks for payment by gift card, crypto or e-transfer to a person
Hang up on calls that threaten arrest or deportation
When in doubt, call the CRA using the number on its official website
Be careful with job offers that ask you to receive and forward money
Can I keep my bank account in my home country? Yes. If your foreign accounts and assets add up to more than $100,000, you may need to report them on your Canadian tax return.
Is it safe to keep money in a Canadian bank? Yes. Eligible deposits at member institutions are protected by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
Do I pay tax on money I bring with me? Generally no. Money you bring when you move is not income. Income you earn after you become a resident, in Canada or abroad, must be reported.
What is the cheapest way to send money home? It depends on the amount and the country. Compare the fee and the exchange rate together.

about.title: About MapleSteps | MapleSteps
about.desc: Who runs MapleSteps, how the site is funded, and how we handle your privacy.
about.lead: MapleSteps is a free, independent guide for newcomers to Canada, written in plain language and available in six languages.

sections.p: We are an independent website. We are not part of the Government of Canada or any immigration agency, and we do not give legal or immigration advice. For your own situation, contact a settlement agency or an authorized professional.

MapleSteps is free because of advertising. Some pages may include affiliate links. If you buy through one, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend things we believe help newcomers.
Found a mistake or have a suggestion? Email hello@maplesteps.ca.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy | MapleSteps
privacy.desc: How MapleSteps handles your information, cookies and advertising, including Google AdSense, and how to opt out of personalized ads.
privacy.lead: Last updated: November 7, 2026. This policy explains what information is collected when you visit maplesteps.ca and how it is used.

sections.p: MapleSteps (maplesteps.ca) is an independent website that publishes free guides for newcomers to Canada. It is not a government website.
You can use MapleSteps without creating an account or giving us any personal information. If you email us, we receive your email address and your message, and we use them only to reply to you.

Ticks on the first-steps checklist and your language choice are saved only in your own browser (local storage). They are not sent to us. You can clear them at any time with the "Clear my checklist" button or in your browser settings.

MapleSteps is free because it shows ads. Third-party vendors, including Google, use cookies to serve ads based on your prior visits to this website or other websites. Google's use of advertising cookies enables it and its partners to serve ads to you based on your visits to this site and/or other sites on the internet.

sections.h: How to opt out of personalized ads
sections.p: You can turn off personalized advertising in Google's Ads Settings. You can also opt out of other vendors' use of cookies for personalized advertising at youradchoices.ca (Canada) or aboutads.info. In some regions, including the European Economic Area and the United Kingdom, you will be asked for your consent before personalized ads are shown.

The site is hosted by Cloudflare, which processes basic technical data, such as IP addresses, to deliver pages and protect the site from attacks. We may use privacy-friendly statistics to count visits. We do not sell personal information.
Our guides link to government and other websites. Those sites have their own privacy policies, which we encourage you to read.
MapleSteps is written for adults. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children.
We may update this policy from time to time. The date at the top shows the latest version. If you have questions about your privacy, email hello@maplesteps.ca.
